This document tracks profiling insights, baseline/post-optimization metrics, Mastodon-specific testing gotchas, and the roadmap across optimization phases (`spec/models`, `spec/requests`, and `spec/fabricators`).

## Profiling Commands Used

All profiling used `test-prof` (already in `Gemfile`) and `stackprof`:

```bash
# Full profiling breakdown (factories, setup vs body, SQL queries, wall-time flamegraph)
FPROF=1 RD_PROF=1 RD_PROF_TOP=25 EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record EVENT_PROF_TOP=25 TEST_STACK_PROF=wall \
  bundle exec rspec -r test_prof spec/models --format progress

# Inspect StackProf wall-time dump
bundle exec stackprof tmp/test_prof/stack-prof-report-wall-raw-total.dump --text --limit 40
bundle exec stackprof tmp/test_prof/stack-prof-report-wall-raw-total.dump --text --sort-total --limit 60
```

---

## Phase 1: `spec/models` (Completed)

### Summary of Results

| Stage | `spec/models` Time (1,795 exs) | Improvement vs Baseline | SQL Queries (`sql.active_record`) | Factory Calls (total / top-level) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Baseline** (seed 18415) | **124.1s (2m 4.1s)** | — | ~113,956 | 4,721 / 3,243 |
| **Step 1:** Remove leftover `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` + set `config.log_level = 'warn'` in `config/environments/test.rb` | **65.05s** | **-47.6% (1.91x)** | 113,956 | 4,721 / 3,243 |
| **Step 2:** Default `type: :model` to `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)` with `:sidekiq_inline` tag opt-in | **48.76s** | **-60.7% (2.55x)** | 71,068 (-37.6%) | 4,721 / 3,243 |
| **Step 3:** Enable TestProf `let_it_be` / `before_all` (`spec/support/test_prof.rb`) and restructure shared setup in top 27 slow model specs | **31.87s – 34.61s (~33.4s)** | **-73.1% (~3.7x)** | **41,889 (-63.2%)** | **2,540 / 1,763 (-46.2%)** |

### Root Causes Found & Fixed in Phase 1

1. **Global `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` accidentally left in a spec file (~30% of total suite time!)**
   - `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb:6` executed `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` at class/file load time.
   - Because it ran during spec loading, it enabled verbose query backtrace cleaning (`ActiveSupport::BacktraceCleaner#first_clean_frame` / `Thread.each_caller_location`) on **every SQL query across the entire RSpec process** (affecting all spec directories whenever that file was loaded).
   - StackProf wall-time share before fix: **34.1%** in `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` (29.8% in `log_query_source` / `BacktraceCleaner`), writing ~65 MB per run to `log/test.log`.

2. **Test environment log level defaulted to `:debug` (~5–8s + massive disk I/O)**
   - `config/environments/test.rb` did not set `config.log_level`, so Rails defaulted to `:debug`, causing `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql`, `ActiveJob::LogSubscriber`, etc., to colorize, filter, format bind params, and write every query to `log/test.log`.
   - Fix: set `config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', 'warn')` in `config/environments/test.rb`. Rails 8.1 `ActiveSupport::LogSubscriber` checks `silenced?(event)` against `subscribe_log_level` before invoking `sql(event)`. Can still be overridden with `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`.
   - Verified no specs break (only `spec/models/concerns/remotable_spec.rb` asserts `Rails.logger.debug`, using `allow(Rails.logger).to receive(:debug)`, which still works).

3. **Global `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` executing `TriggerWebhookWorker` on every record save (~26% of post-log-fix time)**
   - `spec/rails_helper.rb` forced `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` globally before every example.
   - Every local `Status`, `User`, `Account`, or `Report` create/update enqueued `TriggerWebhookWorker`, which immediately ran synchronously -> `WebhookService#call` -> `WebhookService#serialize_event` (full `REST::Admin::WebhookEventSerializer` JSON serialization with many N+1 queries) **even when zero `Webhook` records exist in the DB**.

     - Only **3 model spec blocks** needed the `:sidekiq_inline` tag (all testing `deliver_later` email delivery via `capture_emails`):
       - `spec/models/email_subscription_spec.rb` (`describe 'Callbacks', :sidekiq_inline`)
       - `spec/models/user_spec.rb` (`describe '#mark_email_as_confirmed!', :sidekiq_inline`)
       - `spec/models/admin/account_action_spec.rb` (`it 'sends email to target account user', :sidekiq_inline`)
     - Note: `rspec-sidekiq` already runs `Sidekiq::Worker.clear_all` in `before(:each)` by default.

- **Actual HTTP request execution** (`ActionDispatch` -> Controller -> Serializer/View -> PostgreSQL) is now ~20s (~10.6ms/request across 1,877 examples) — a healthy floor where Phase 3 factory optimizations will cleanly push `spec/requests` below ~30s and `spec/models` below ~20s!

## Phase 3 Plan: Factories (`spec/fabricators/`) (Next)

Profiling both `spec/models` and `spec/requests` confirmed that built-in factory bloat (untouched in Phases 1 & 2 per instructions) is now the single largest remaining bottleneck across **both** suites (~10–12s in `spec/models` + ~10–12s in `spec/requests`):

1. **`spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb` (HIGHEST IMPACT):**
   - Contains `after_create { |status| Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status) }`!
   - Every single `Fabricate(:status)` secretly creates a `Bookmark` -> a brand-new `Account` -> a brand-new `User` -> 2 `LoginActivity` records + a BCrypt password hash!
   - Even *after* Phases 1 & 2 `let_it_be` optimizations, hidden `bookmark` creation still accounts for **410 calls / 4.48s** in `spec/models` and **294 calls / 3.40s** in `spec/requests` (~8s combined!).
   - Removing this unconditional `after_create` bookmark (adding it only where a spec explicitly needs a bookmark) will roughly halve the cost of `Fabricate(:status)` everywhere.
2. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb`:**
   - Contains `after_create { |user| 2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity, user: user) } }` — creates 2 unnecessary `LoginActivity` rows on every `User` (and every local `Account`) — still **714 hidden calls** in `spec/requests` and hundreds in `spec/models`.
   - Uses `password '123456789'`, triggering `BCrypt::Engine.__bc_crypt` (clamped at cost 4, ~1.5ms/call) on every single `User` and local `Account` (~2.0s in `spec/models`, ~1.5s in `spec/requests`). Pre-computing `encrypted_password` once at load time (using `Devise::Encryptor.digest(User, '123456789')`) when `password` is not explicitly overridden will eliminate ~99% of BCrypt CPU time while preserving full password authentication compatibility.
3. **`spec/fabricators/account_fabricator.rb`:**

Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil) : nil }`), which runs `User#set_approved` (`UsernameBlock.matches?`, `EmailDomainBlock.requires_approval?`, `UserRole.everyone`, `UnreservedUsernameValidator`, `UniqueUsernameValidator`), BCrypt, and 2x `LoginActivity`.
   - Optimizing `user_fabricator` immediately speeds up every local `Account`, and auditing whether some specs/fabricators even need a `User` for every local `Account` can save even more.
4. **`spec/fabricators/media_attachment_fabricator.rb`:**

We have a total of 2540 factories being created in this suite, with 1763 being top-level, and it's taking a substantial chunk of our test time – 21.6 seconds out of a total of 30.6 seconds. That's a whopping 70.5% of the time spent on factory creation alone! Clearly, we have some serious bottlenecks to address.

Let's break this down. The `status` factory is taking a solid 6.94 seconds, which is significant, but it pales in comparison to `bookmark` which takes 3.92s! Interestingly, the vast majority of these `bookmark` calls are *nested* within the `status` factory, which explains the high count: 414 total, but only 4 top-level!

Then, the `account` factory is also proving to be costly, clocking in at 4.85 seconds. Interestingly, `media_attachment` also is a concern, with 4.51s for 23 calls, a significant per-call time - specifically the `Terrapin::MultiPipeExtensions#read` method is the source of 3.8s of that time!

The `user`, `admin_user`, and `moderator_user` group is about 1.11 seconds for ~107 calls, but there is some complexity here as `account` is building `user` objects. This is where things get interesting: `login_activity` is also a concern, 206 total, but 0 top-level calls. So `account` has a `Fabricate.build(:user)` call in it. *Wait!* I need to verify: does `after_create` in `user_fabricator` even run when using `Fabricate.build(:user)`? I know `Fabricate.build` doesn't seem to invoke the `after_create` hooks, and it looks like this is the case here. This is why we are getting a BCrypt performance hit - it's running on EVERY build, even local builds inside other factories, whereas top-level `Fabricate` calls are running `2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity) }` which is showing in this breakdown.

Finally, we have `preview_card` and `preview_card_trend`, which are taking 0.58 seconds combined, likely due to image attachment processing. `custom_emoji` also contributes with 0.38 seconds with image processing. The rest of the factories, like `notification`, `report`, `status_trend`, and `follow` seem less problematic in comparison.

steps.reasoning_content:
**Investigating Performance Bottlenecks in the Test Suite**

Okay, good thing I started by checking those `linked_data_signature_spec.rb` and `process_account_service_spec.rb` specs! I see in the first one, line 91, that the spec *assumes* the `Fabricate(:account)` factory stores keys in `keypairs` and not `public_key`. And the same assumption is made in the second spec at line 262, when they delete all of Alice's `keypairs`. I need to figure out why `keypairs` are costing us 2.14ms.

Looking into `account_fabricator.rb`, it seems that creating a `Keypair` row is always happening, even though `legacy_keypair` is a transient flag.  That's because `Keypair` encrypts the `private_key` with AES-256-GCM. I notice the database queries include a select followed by insert query.

Now, I'm thinking about broader implications: what about other specs, like `mastodon/cli/accounts_spec.rb`, `object_integrity_proof_spec.rb`, and `process_account_service_spec.rb`? There were only 17 files in the whole repo that mentioned `keypair`! Should I change the default for `legacy_keypair` in the `account_fabricator`? I need to be *extremely* careful. If I change the default, I could break specs in `spec/lib/`, `spec/services/`, and `spec/controllers/` even if I only measure performance in `spec/models` and `spec/requests`.  Factories are shared. That would be a huge bug! So, if I change it, I have to check those files, or maybe it's better to leave `account_fabricator` as it is.

But before I commit to changing *anything* with `keypairs`, I need to inspect other bottlenecks first. Let's see...

1.  `app/models/user.rb`: Why is `User` executing the `SELECT "user_roles"` query TWICE? And why is it taking 3.6ms even *without* considering the bcrypt hashing?
2.  `spec/models/media_attachment_spec.rb` is taking 5.07s!  I should check the fabricator, too.
3.  I should also check `preview_card_fabricator.rb` and `custom_emoji_fabricator.rb`.
4.  And don't forget that `account_fabricator.rb` creates a `user` on every local `Account`!
5.  I have to look at the other fabricators and the slowest specs in `spec/models` and `spec/requests`.

First, I need to check `app/models/user.rb` around `role`, `UserRole`, and the callbacks. I'll start there.

# frozen_string_literal: true

module Paperclip
  class LazyThumbnail < Paperclip::Thumbnail
    def make
      return File.open(@file.path) unless needs_convert?

      if options[:geometry]
        min_side = [@current_geometry.width, @current_geometry.height].min.to_i
        options[:geometry] = "#{min_side}x#{min_side}#" if @target_geometry.square? && min_side < @target_geometry.width
      elsif options[:pixels]
        width  = Math.sqrt(options[:pixels] * (@current_geometry.width.to_f / @current_geometry.height)).round.to_i
        height = Math.sqrt(options[:pixels] * (@current_geometry.height.to_f / @current_geometry.width)).round.to_i
        options[:geometry] = "#{width}x#{height}>"
      end

      Paperclip::Thumbnail.make(file, options, attachment)
    end

    private

    def needs_convert?
      needs_different_geometry? || needs_different_format? || needs_metadata_stripping?
    end

    def needs_different_geometry?
      (options[:geometry] && @current_geometry.width != @target_geometry.width && @current_geometry.height != @target_geometry.height) ||
        (options[:pixels] && @current_geometry.width * @current_geometry.height > options[:pixels])
    end

    def needs_different_format?
      @format.present? && @current_format != @format
    end

    def needs_metadata_stripping?
      @attachment.instance.respond_to?(:local?) && @attachment.instance.local?
    end
  end
end

steps.reasoning_content:
**Performance Optimization Eureka!**

Okay, here's the deal. I was digging into some performance bottlenecks and stumbled upon something big. Initially, I was looking at `custom_emoji_batch_spec.rb` and `cli/emoji_spec.rb` because those are the only two instances that *actually* need the file on disk. The rest can get away with using something transient. But then I saw that `Fabricate(:custom_emoji)` was taking a whopping 40ms! Turns out, that's because it was triggering ImageMagick's `convert` for every single instance. The root cause? `emojo.png` is a local file, so the thumbnailing logic kicked in needlessly.

The fix? Default the `custom_emoji_fabricator` to set `image_file_name`, `image_content_type`, `image_file_size`, and `image_updated_at`. If we can, include a `Fabricator(:custom_emoji_with_image)` or make the file transient. By doing this we can see that Fabricate's performance goes from 40ms to 0.8ms – that's a 50x speedup!

Now, this got me thinking. I did the same check for `media_attachment_fabricator.rb`! It's used ALL over the place, and I started checking callers of `Fabricate(:media_attachment)` across all of spec.

I found several slow spots:

In `spec/models`:
*   `spec/models/status_spec.rb` had four calls, each taking 114ms just to create a media attachment. None of them needed a real file.
*   `spec/models/media_attachment_spec.rb` itself was a goldmine of inefficiency. One line ran twice taking 228ms that didn't need the file!  Other lines had several slow calls to attachment_fixture with specific files to test specific cases. There's a particular MP3 that took a whopping 2.65 seconds! Turns out, that's testing an mp3 with cover art, so that's actually valid as it's testing a specific case.

In `spec/requests`:
*   Quite a few calls in requests that are just using the file needlessly.

Now, a crucial piece:  I looked at `spec/fabricators/media_attachment_fabricator.rb` and saw this: the `file` block. So the issue is that it's *always* creating an attachment. But, like with the custom emojis, some specs DO need it.

So, the next step is to methodically go through EVERY single spec that calls `Fabricate.*:media_attachment` *without* passing a `file:` argument. We need to identify which specs genuinely need the file and which ones are just needlessly incurring this performance hit. We can then either make the file transient or, in a couple of cases, pass the file with the `file:` option.

Okay, hold on a second! 83 calls to `Fabricate(:media_attachment)`?! That's a lot, and it's a huge red flag because I'm guessing a vast majority of those calls don't actually need to interact with a real, processed file on disk. Let's take a look at `media_attachment_fabricator.rb` and see what's going on.

Ah, here it is: the `file` attribute is dependent on the `type`. We use `attachment_fixture('attachment.webm')` or `attachment_fixture('attachment.jpg')` depending on if the type is a video or a GIF. The current implementation is inefficient, and I think I've got a way to significantly speed things up.

The key is in how those metadata columns (`file_file_name`, `file_content_type`, `file_file_size`, `file_updated_at`, `file_meta`, `blurhash`, `processing`) are populated. What if we were to populate those directly within the `Fabricate(:media_attachment)` call, **unless** a `file:` argument is explicitly passed, or we have a fast default fabrication and then a specific flag, such as `with_file: true` in the few cases where it's absolutely necessary? **A Deep Dive into Test Performance: Uncovering Bottlenecks**

Okay, so I've been digging into these StackProf results, and I'm seeing some significant improvements! The disappearance of `BCrypt::Engine.__bc_crypt` and `Vips.vips_cache_operation_build` from the top 25 is huge! That, combined with the impressive drop in factory time (42.1%!) and SQL queries (16.4%) is fantastic progress. But, as an expert, I know we can't rest on our laurels. My mind is racing with ways to further optimize.

First, I need to focus on these persistent bottlenecks. Both `spec/models` and `spec/requests` are still showing substantial time spent on `account` and `user` creation – roughly 7.5 seconds in models and 7 seconds in requests. The profile data gives me the precise query counts and times for the calls in both sets of specs. Specifically:

*   In `spec/models`, `account` is taking 4.36 seconds across 532 calls, `status` takes 3.02 seconds across 394 calls, and `user` is taking 0.66 seconds across 90 calls.
*   In `spec/requests`, `account` takes 2.80 seconds across 401 calls, `status` takes 1.95 seconds across 285 calls, and `user` + `admin_user` take 2.31 seconds across 354 calls.

This is where I'm going to start my optimization.

**Question 1: The Fabricator Mystery**

My first question is: Why is `Fabricate(:account)` taking **7.0–8.2ms** and executing **9 SQL queries**? It looks like the account uniqueness validation, username blocks, email uniqueness, email domain blocks, and those `user_roles` calls are killing us! I need to trace this back.

Then, there's the question of the multiple factory calls...

**Question 2: User Role Madness**

Then, I'm thinking... those queries to `user_roles` are suspect. Two selects per `user` creation (queries 4 & 5)! Why is the `User` model fetching that role information twice? It seems that in the case where the `role_id` is set to `UserRole.everyone`, the code sets `role = nil`, but then it seems we're pulling the role back again!

And I can't touch the application code directly, so I need to find a way to mitigate that.

**Question 3: Requests & the API**

I see a LOT of calls to `Fabricate(:user)` and `Fabricate(:admin_user)` in `spec/requests` (354 in total), which is a huge number! How can these factory calls be reduced? We have around 110 of them that are due to `include_context` calls, which makes sense. I need to find where the other 244 are coming from.

Furthermore, `spec/support/examples/api.rb` is showing 157 factory calls, with a big cost. I'll need to figure out which request specs are responsible for the calls within `forbidden for wrong scope`/`forbidden for wrong role` scenarios.

**Question 4: Media Attachment's Time**

Then there's `spec/models/media_attachment_spec.rb`, which is clocking in at 4.34 seconds! That's 22% of the whole model run! I need to see what's happening. And I note that `IO.select` is 15.4% of the time. What's taking so long? I need to time every single example in that file to pinpoint the culprit.

**Question 5: Keys to Efficiency**

Next, a thought comes to mind related to `remote_account` and key generation. If the `remote_account` skips creating a keypair, does `spec/models` or `spec/requests` care?

**Question 6: Fabricators and Dependencies**

Lastly, I need to look at how fabricators are structured. Consider `Fabricate(:status)`: It builds an `account`, which also builds a `user` with all its attendant queries. Can I make all these fabricators use a built `:user` when creating an `:account`? I need to check the codebase to see how these associations are used. Does `status.account.user` get called?

**Next Steps**

So, here's my plan:

steps.reasoning_content:
**Performance Deep Dive: Identifying and Addressing Slow Tests & Data Creation Bottlenecks**

Okay, hold on a second! My internal radar is screaming. I'm looking at `spec/models/media_attachment_spec.rb` and the numbers are glaring. Nearly half a second just to test a simple file presence check? Let's break this down. Line 45 to 64 is using `avatar.gif` (FFmpeg/Vips invoked!) TWICE to test `file.blank? && remote_url.present?`. We can replace this with a faster fixture like `attachment_fixture('emojo.png')` to save a whopping **0.58 seconds** cleanly! And the next offender, line 270, takes **0.391 seconds**! It looks like we're calling `Fabricate(:media_attachment)` (full FFmpeg H.264/AAC transcoding!) just to validate a size limit. We can probably just `Fabricate.build(:media_attachment, ...)` and build the object, and then check `valid?`. I should also investigate why line 264 took only 68ms while 270 was 391ms.

Line 258 also takes a significant amount of time, but that's likely just first-example overhead, which is fine! Line 244 with `boop.mp3` and its large cover art is expected because it's *supposed* to be slow; it's asserting the actual transcoding. We can't touch that one.

steps.reasoning_content:
**A Mastodon Invariant Discovered!**

Aha! This experiment has been incredibly valuable! Those four failure groups have revealed a critical invariant in Mastodon's architecture. Let me break this down:

1.  In `activitypub/replies_spec.rb`, the `Account` controllers are specifically checking for the presence of a `User` associated with the account, particularly in cases of local accounts, and returning a 404 if there's no `User`! This is key. We need to look at `#unavailable?` or `#searchable`!
2.  `api/v1/statuses_spec.rb:285` has logic that similarly relies on the quoted status having a user on its account.
3.  The admin report page, `admin/reports_spec.rb`, also makes use of the `target_account.user` property.
4.  Finally, `api/v1/directories_spec.rb` joins `:user` through the `account_stat`'s associated account.

This highlights the issue: a local `Account` in Mastodon *always* has a `User`! My hunch is that this is baked into the fundamental design. Checking `app/controllers/concerns/account_controller_concern.rb` and `app/models/concerns/account/associations.rb` would likely confirm this.  If `account.user_approved?` returns a falsy value when `user` is nil, that's already a problem. The act of setting `user: nil` in fabricators like `status_fabricator`, `report_fabricator`, and `account_stat_fabricator` is breaking this crucial invariant. It will lead to inconsistencies and errors!

Therefore, my immediate course of action is to undo the problematic changes to keep Steps 1 and 2 intact, and keep the others out:  Specifically, I'm going to revert Step 3 - specifically the child fabricators modified. I'll use `git checkout` on the affected files, while carefully checking `git diff --stat` to make sure I don't accidentally undo the beneficial changes from steps 1 and 2. We can preserve steps 1 and 2, but revert 3, to verify this invariant and rectify any violations.

**Optimizing Factory Usage in `spec/models`**

Okay, here's what's going through my mind as I analyze these specs. I see a massive opportunity for optimization in how we use factories, specifically within the `spec/models` directory.

Firstly, looking at `spec/models/notification_spec.rb`, particularly lines 166-266, I'm struck by the unnecessary duplication. In sections like lines 169-172 and 199-202, we're creating a slew of `Status`, `Account`, and `User` objects—**16** of each to be exact! And in lines 247-265, for each notification type, we're creating an additional 2-3 `Account`s and `User`s (~**18** in a single example!). Similarly, lines 62-164 are doing the same things - there is a complete duplication. This is where I realize that by sharing a single `account` and `other_account` via `let_it_be`, we could dramatically reduce this bloat to a total of **2** Accounts. A similar approach can be used for `.paginate_groups_by_max_id` and `.paginate_groups_by_min_id` and this reduces 18 to 2 Accounts! We're often building in-memory notifications for testing, so this pattern is ideal.

Now, let's look at the broader picture and formulate a 'Wave 3' optimization strategy for factory usage across `spec/models`:

1.  **`spec/models/media_attachment_spec.rb`**: We can optimize this quickly. Replacing the animated `avatar.gif` with `mini-static.gif` for the `needs_redownload?` test will save significant time (**0.54s**!). Also, for `size limit validation`, we should be using `Fabricate.build` instead of a full fabrication.
2.  **`spec/models/account/avatar_spec.rb` & `spec/models/account/header_spec.rb`**: Here, we can introduce `let_it_be(:account)` to share read-only account examples in both files.
3.  **`spec/models/trends/statuses_spec.rb`**: The strategy here is to reuse `reblog_accounts` (eliminating **35 redundant Account + User fabrications**!).
4.  **`spec/models/notification_spec.rb`**: This is a core focus, as we've already identified the potential to eliminate **~50** unnecessary `Account` and `User` fabrications by sharing accounts.
5.  **`spec/models/status_spec.rb`**: Similarly, we'll pass `account:` to statuses, polls, and media attachments and so on to eliminate **~30+** redundant `Account` and `User` fabrications.
6.  **`spec/models/public_feed_spec.rb`**: Focus here will be to pass `account: account` to statuses and share `let_it_be(:local_account)` / `let_it_be(:remote_account)` / `let_it_be(:other_account)` across the tests.
7.  **`spec/models/report_spec.rb`**: Re-use of `let_it_be(:account)` + `let_it_be(:target_account)` (passes `account:` to all 8 `action_log` fabrications!) will streamline things.

I'm starting by carefully inspecting `spec/models/featured_tag_spec.rb` and `spec/models/report_spec.rb` (lines 1-90) to make sure these edits are surgically precise and to make sure I am being the most effective. The goal is to make these tests lean and efficient!

steps.message: Let's run `spec/requests` cleanly (unprofiled) to measure our Wave 4 progress!
steps.reasoning_content:
Here's my take on this, considering I'm deep in the weeds of performance testing:

**Holy Smokes! That's Fast!**

Okay, so 244 examples in 3.14 seconds *with* zero failures on the initial attempt? That's impressive! A very promising first pass. This warrants a more in depth look.

My immediate thought is to run the entire `spec/requests` suite, *without* any profiling to get a clean baseline. That'll give us an idea of the raw speed. But that's not enough; we need the granular data to understand what just happened.

I need to dig deeper. Let's fire up a full profile run, setting `FPROF=1` *and* `EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record`. I want to see a full flame graph using the most expensive events. That will reveal where the bottlenecks actually are within `spec/requests`. Specifically, I'm eager to get a handle on the database interaction because that's usually where things get hairy. This is going to tell me exactly how well `spec/requests` did *and* point the way to further refinements.

arguments.command: bundle exec rspec spec/requests --format progress --seed 23323

steps.message: Let's run `FPROF=1 EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record` on `spec/models` to capture detailed post-optimization factory and SQL metrics.
steps.reasoning_content:
**My Immediate Reaction to the Optimization Results**

Wow! Just... *wow*. 30.35 seconds for all 1,877 request examples. That's a significant drop from the previous 44.06 seconds - a whopping -31.1% improvement! This is even better than anticipated. Let me break down the individual components:

*   The `spec/models` suite is clocking in at around 18.9-19.3 seconds, a fantastic -41.5% reduction from the original 32.74 seconds.
*   The `spec/requests` suite, the one I was most focused on, has improved from 44.06 seconds to 30.35 seconds, a respectable -31.1% gain.
*   And combined, we're looking at a total time of ~49.5 seconds, down from 76.80 seconds. That’s a staggering -35.5% reduction! This blows past the 10-20% target we were aiming for!

Okay, this is excellent. However, let's not get complacent. There might be some low-hanging fruit still available to us. Now, I want to run `FPROF=1 EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record` on *both* `spec/models` and `spec/requests` separately. This will give us precise factory and SQL metrics after optimization. This way, we can make sure there aren't any sneaky spots for further improvement that we're missing. Let's start with `spec/models`.

steps.reasoning_content:
**Initial Observations & Excitement**

Okay, *whoa*! Just taking a look at `spec/models`... Even with full profiling enabled (`FPROF=1 EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record`), this suite is *flying*! It finished in a blistering **20.02s**! That's impressive, especially considering it was clocking in around 18.5s without the profiling overhead.

The big win is clearly the factory time. We've gone from **21.61s down to 12.66s** – a whopping **41.4%** improvement! And a big chunk of that factory time, 3.87s, is *actually* the ffmpeg/vips tests in `media_attachment_spec`, which includes `boop.mp3` taking up 2.64s.

Diving deeper, the improvements are across the board: `status` went from **6.94s to 1.99s** (-71.4%!), `notification` from **0.57s to 0.16s** (-72%!), `report` from **0.44s to 0.17s** (-61%!), `preview_card` + `preview_card_trend` from **0.58s to 0.05s** (-91%!), and `custom_emoji` from **0.38s to 0.065s** (-83%!). And the SQL event count has dropped from 41,889 to 28,123 (-32.9%!!).

Okay, that's incredibly encouraging. Now, I need to see if we can replicate these gains in `spec/requests`... let's run `FPROF=1 EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record` on that suite and see what happens!

steps.reasoning_content:
**Optimization Results Are INCREDIBLE!**

Wow, just... wow! Take a look at this `spec/requests` table! I'm absolutely floored by these results. We've significantly reduced factory calls; going from 2,914 down to 1,517 - that's a *47.9%* reduction, nearly halving the number! Even the top-level factory calls saw a decent drop from 1,870 to 1,474 (-21.2%).

The factory time is even more impressive – dropping from a staggering 17.36 seconds to a much more manageable 8.41 seconds, a whopping 51.6% decrease, more than halving that time! Looking at the breakdown, the improvements across the board are substantial, `status` went from 5.08s to 1.97s (-61.2%), `account` from 3.77s to 1.83s (-51.5%) with a reduced number of calls!, `user` + `admin_user` went from 3.79s to 2.17s (-42.7%) with a reduced number of calls, `bookmark` basically vanished (294 to 2, a 99.3% reduction!), and `login_activity` is now zero calls, and the `media_attachment` dropped from 0.76s to 0.14s (-81.6%) and `preview_card` went from 0.39s to 0.02s (-95%). Some other areas saw improvements as well! `collection` dropped from 76 to 44, `domain_block` from 38 to 25 and `email_domain_block` from 30 to 6.

And SQL queries! We've cut that down too! A total of 14,480 queries were eliminated, dropping from 65,363 to 50,883, a -22.2% reduction.

Okay, now it's time to tie up loose ends. Let's start by cleaning up those temporary scripts in `/tmp/` – gotta keep things tidy! Then I'll run RuboCop across all the modified files to ensure 100% code style and linting compliance. Next, I need to update `docs/rspec_optimization.md` with a complete Phase 3 update, including baseline metrics, the post-optimization results, insights and potential gotchas. Finally, the ultimate test: I need to run those final clean, unprofiled benchmarks on both `spec/models` and `spec/requests` using multiple seeds to make sure we've eliminated any order-dependence or flakiness. Oh, and I definitely need to verify the specs outside of models/requests as well!

First things first, checking the `git status` and running RuboCop on any modified Ruby files! Time to get to work!

## Phase 3 Plan: Factories (`spec/fabricators/`) (Next)

Profiling both `spec/models` and `spec/requests` confirmed that built-in factory bloat (untouched in Phases 1 & 2 per instructions) is now the single largest remaining bottleneck across **both** suites (~10–12s in `spec/models` + ~10–12s in `spec/requests`):

1. **`spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb` (HIGHEST IMPACT):**
   - Contains `after_create { |status| Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status) }`!
   - Every single `Fabricate(:status)` secretly creates a `Bookmark` -> a brand-new `Account` -> a brand-new `User` -> 2 `LoginActivity` records + a BCrypt password hash!
   - Even *after* Phases 1 & 2 `let_it_be` optimizations, hidden `bookmark` creation still accounts for **410 calls / 4.48s** in `spec/models` and **294 calls / 3.40s** in `spec/requests` (~8s combined!).
   - Removing this unconditional `after_create` bookmark (adding it only where a spec explicitly needs a bookmark) will roughly halve the cost of `Fabricate(:status)` everywhere.
2. **`spec/fabricators/user_fabricator.rb`:**
   - Contains `after_create { |user| 2.times { Fabricate(:login_activity, user: user) } }` — creates 2 unnecessary `LoginActivity` rows on every `User` (and every local `Account`) — still **714 hidden calls** in `spec/requests` and hundreds in `spec/models`.

Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil) : nil }`), which runs `User#set_approved` (`UsernameBlock.matches?`, `EmailDomainBlock.requires_approval?`, `UserRole.everyone`, `UnreservedUsernameValidator`, `UniqueUsernameValidator`), BCrypt, and 2x `LoginActivity`.

   - `spec/fabricators/accessible_access_token_fabricator.rb`: added `last_used_at { Time.now.utc }` so tokens created outside `'with API authentication'` also avoid `AccessTokenTrackingConcern` `UPDATE oauth_access_tokens` writes on every request.

     - `trends/statuses_spec.rb`, `notification_spec.rb`, `status_spec.rb`, `public_feed_spec.rb`, `report_spec.rb`, `fasp/backfill_request_spec.rb`, `concerns/account/mappings_spec.rb`, `export_spec.rb`, `featured_tag_spec.rb`: reused shared `let_it_be` accounts across multi-status / multi-action_log / multi-notification setups instead of implicitly fabricating dozens of throwaway `Account` + `User` pairs.

  - Test execution + assertions across 1,795 examples: **~7.5s**.
- **`spec/requests` (~32.0s total):**
  - Factories: **8.41s** (~26% of runtime, down from 17.36s in Phase 3 baseline and 103.8s in Phase 2 baseline!).
  - Actual HTTP request execution (`ActionDispatch` -> Controller -> Serializer/View -> PostgreSQL) across 1,877 examples: **~23s** (~12ms/request).
